title: How Christians Interpret the Bible
author: Modern
content:
HOW CHRISTIANS INTERPRET THE BIBLE

Definitions
:

Christian
: any individual or group which sincerely defines themselves to be
Christian. This would include 
Mormons
, 
Jehovah's
Witnesses
 and even some 
Unitarian Universalists
. Many Christians use
other definitions and consider groups which differ significantly from themselves (or from
historical Christianity) to be non-Christians - or even 
cults
.

CT
: Conservative theologians and their beliefs

LT
: Liberal theologians and their beliefs

All Christians recognize the Hebrew and Christian Scriptures (Old and New Testament) as their
prime source of religious beliefs. However, various Christian groups and individuals approach the
Bible with different assumptions. This causes them to develop 
very
 divergent beliefs and
practices.

Three common ways of approaching the Scriptures are:

CT
: Conservative Christians (Fundamentalists and other Evangelicals) usually have four
fundamental assumptions:

The Bible is inerrant. That is, when the 66 books were originally written, God prevented
the writers from making any errors whatsoever.

All passages in the Bible are equally valid and are useful as a spiritual guide; the 
"Word
of God"
 is totally consistent, and was as valid at the time of Adam and Eve as it is today.

Each passage of the Bible should be interpreted literally where possible.

English versions of the Bible are reliable translations, particularly the King James Version
(KJV) and New International Version (NIV).

LT
: Liberal Christians (e.g. many members of the United Church of Christ, the United
Church of Canada, the liberal wings of the Episcopal Church and other denominations) view
the Bible differently:

The Bible was written by authors who promoted differing religious views, reflecting the
evolution of religious thought over about a 10 century time span. (e.g. Jehovah was prone to
ordering genocidal attacks on neighboring tribes in the Hebrew Scriptures. In the Christian
Scriptures, God is described as loving people of all cultures).

Being human, the authors sometimes made mistakes. (e.g. a number of references to Jewish
religious customs in Luke are in error).

Some forgeries have been added since the original texts were written; accidental errors
have occurred in copying. (Mark 16:9-20 is a famous example of a forgery)

Some parts of the Bible should be ignored and are not suitable as a guide to modern living.
(Laws regulating slavery is one example).

The Bible contains much material adsorbed from neighboring Pagan cultures and pre-Abramic
beliefs (e.g. one of the creation stories in Genesis, and the Noahic flood).

Bible passages have to be interpreted according to the beliefs of the writers and their
culture (e.g. Paul's comments restricting women's activity in church).

Modern versions of the Bible are reasonably accurate translations of the original Hebrew,
Aramaic and Greek, but still reflect the prejudices of the translators, and the belief systems
of the religious institutions which sponsored them. Older translations, like the KJV, are less
reliable because the translators had less complete knowledge of Hebrew, and had access to fewer
ancient manuscripts.

Recent findings of the physical, social and medical sciences have shown that some parts of
the Bible cannot be considered accurate. (e.g. the creation stories, mental illness caused by
demon infestation, etc.).

Midrash Interpretation
: This is a method of looking at the Bible from 
a totally different perspective. As explained by Bishop J.S. Spong (1):

"Midrash is the Jewish way of saying that everything to be venerated in the present must
somehow be connected with a sacred moment in the past...It is the means whereby the experience
of the present can be affirmed and asserted as true inside the symbols of yesterday."

Bishop Spong illustrates Midrash by citing four stories in the Hebrew Scriptures which involved
a common miraculous theme: the parting of waters in a sea or river:

The first story is found in Exodus 14:5-28. The Hebrew people were trapped between the Red
Sea and the approaching Egyptian army. Moses cried out to God who parted the sea so that
the Israelites could pass in safety, with a wall of water on each side of them, and dry seabed
under their feet.

The second story is found in Joshua 3:14-17. Joshua was the successor to Moses. He commanded
that the ark of the covenant be carried to the Jordan River. As the priests who carried the
ark reached the river, God stopped the water and caused it to pile 
"up in a heap a great
distance away."
 (NIV) The priests found themselves standing on dry land.

The third story is found in 2 Kings 2:7-8. In the presence of Elisha, Elijah took his cloak,
rolled it up and struck the water of the River Jordan. 
"The water divided to the right and to
the left, and the two of them crossed over on dry ground."
 (NIV) At this point, Elijah was
taken in a fiery chariot pulled by fiery horses up to heaven. Elisha was left behind.

The fourth story is found next in 2 Kings 2:13-14. Elisha picked up Elijah's cloak, struck
the water with it. Again, 
"it divided on the right and to the left and he crossed over."

(NIV). 

According to a Midrash interpretation, the purpose of the parting of the Red Sea was to show
the Israelites that God was on their side and that Moses could call on him for protection. The
purpose of the second, third and fourth stories was to show that God continued to work through
his chosen prophets in later times. They also show that the history of Israel is continuous,
containing repetitive themes that link back to earlier events.

It is not useful to ask whether the partings of the waters actually occurred. A proper question
is (2) 

"What was the experience that led, or even compelled, the compilers of sacred tradition to
include this moment, this life or this event inside the interpretive framework of their sacred
past?"

Interpretations of Typical Passages

Examples of the 
CT, LT
 and 
Midrash
 interpretations of the same Biblical
passage are described below. They are intended to illustrate how devout, thoughtful and
intelligent Christians can arrive at totally different understandings of the same verses:

The Parting of the Waters

CT
: Moses, Joshua, Elijah and Elisha actually called upon God to part the waters. The
water was physically separated, with (at least in the first three stories) dry land under
foot. These were miraculous events that happened at a specific time and location. God
temporarily suspended normal physical laws, such as gravity, and the ability of the sea/river
bed to adsorb water.

LT
: No miracles occurred in ancient times. If the waters actually did separate, the
event was caused by natural forces. Perhaps a strong wind drove the Red Sea away from its normal
shoreline. Perhaps a tidal wave generated by a volcano temporarily disturbed the Red Sea. (3)
Perhaps an earthquake damned up the Jordan river and stopped its flow for a few hours. (4)
(The latter phenomenon has been observed six times between 1160 and 1927). Or perhaps the stories
are simply fables.

Midrash Tradition
: As described above, whether these events happened or not was not
important. The stories showed how God worked through various Prophets, and how the present is
linked to the history of the Jewish people.

The Births of John the Baptist and of Jesus Christ

CT
: John's conception happened precisely as described in Luke 1:3-25. A priest
named Zechariah and wife Elizabeth had no children; Elizabeth was infertile and both were old.
The angel Gabriel told the priest that his wife would conceive and bear a son who would

"make ready a people prepared for the Lord."
 (NIV) She did become pregnant and their
son was given the name of John. Both Luke and Matthew described how the Holy Spirit
came upon the 
virgin Mary
 and made her pregnant. The unusual
conception of John and the miraculous conception of Jesus occurred exactly as described in the
gospels.

LT
: John's conception might have happened when his parents were old, but it was
simply an unusual birth. The virgin conception of Jesus did not happen as described in Luke and
Matthew. Jesus had a human father and a mother, and was conceived in the usual manner.

Midrash Tradition
: The Hebrew Scriptures describe four unusual births similar to
John in the Christian Scriptures: Ishmael, Isaac, Samson and Samuel. Usually, prior to the birth,
an angel appears to an individual; the latter is afraid; the message of an upcoming birth is
given; objections are raised; a sign is given; and the birth is considered unusual because
he mother was either old or infertile. John's conception is thus tied to repeating stories of
unusual births during the history of the Jews, in the Midrash tradition. But his conception was
doubly unusual because his mother was 
both
 old 
and
 infertile. This was a Midrash
way of pointing out that John was even more important than any of the four Old Testament figures.
By having Jesus conceived by a virgin, the significance of his conception is raised above that
of John to the status of a true miracle. This is again a Midrash method of implying that Jesus
was much more important than either John or the Old Testament figures.

Other New Testament Events

There are many dozens of events in the Christian Scriptures that mirror events that appeared in
earlier passages of the Bible. Some are:

The guiding stars involved in the births of Abraham, Isaac, Moses and Jesus

The local rulers ordering that Jewish babies be killed, placing both Moses and Jesus at risk.

The temple experiences of Samuel and Jesus

The feeding of 100 men by Elisha and Jesus' feeding of 5000 men plus women and children

Both Elijah and Jesus bringing dead people back to life

The ascension of both Elijah and Jesus up to heaven

History of the Three Interpretive Methods

CT
: The interpretation of the Bible by conservative Christians in the 20th century
is unchanged from that used for almost 2 millennia by the historical Christian church. Until the
15th century CE, essentially all Christians believed that the Bible was inerrant, and that
therefore events happened exactly as described in its text. The astronomical findings of Kepler
and Galileo in the 16th century were the first to seriously threaten this belief system. Further
religious strains occurred in the early 18th century when it became obvious to most
scientists that the earth's geological processes were exceedingly slow, and must have been
accomplished over incredibly long periods of time. Bishop Ussher had predicted that the world
was created in 4004 BCE. This left inadequate time for mountain ranges to erode and others to
build up. Benjamin Franklin proved in the 18th century that lightning is a natural electrical
phenomenon, and not thunderbolts hurled by Satanic powers. The result of such stressors from
scientists caused the Churches to gradually relinquish control of certain beliefs.

LT
: The beliefs and analysis methods of liberal theologians can be traced back to the
start of Biblical "higher criticism" in Germany. It used all of the findings of the social and
natural sciences to examine the Bible and other contemporary religious writings. It rejected
the miracle stories in the Bible and sought natural explanations. Efforts were made to cut
through obscuring passages of the New Testament writings and to reconstruct an accurate image of
Jesus as he existed at the first part of the 1st century CE. Sacred texts of the Christian
Gnostics and other early Christian groups which did not make it into the official canon of the
Christian Scriptures were studied. Sections of the Bible, such as those dealing with slavery and
the suppression of women were rejected as representing a less enlightened social order and the
sexism of Christian leaders. The findings of these religious academics were radical. However,
they did not necessarily filter down to the person in the pew.

Midrash Tradition
: It is fairly obvious that writers of the Hebrew Scriptures employed
Midrash extensively. This tradition seems to have been continued by the writers of the Christian
Scriptures. This would be reasonable to expect, since all but one of the New Testament authors
were of Jewish background and Midrash would form a major part of their religious culture. (The
author of Gospel of Luke and of Acts may have been a Gentile).

Unfortunately, the Roman Army destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 70 CE and dispersed the
Jewish people throughout the rest of the empire. Jewish faith became centered in the local
synagogue and evolved towards a very strict obedience to traditional Jewish belief and practice.
The Jewish Christians were seen as a dangerous breakaway sect. The friction between the early
Christians and mainline Judaism mounted. At the same time, Paul and his followers were
evangelizing the Gentiles (non-Jews). The result was that the Christian movements became
predominately non-Jewish and eventually anti-Semitic. Ignorant of the Midrash tradition and
antagonistic of the Jews, the early Christians began to interpret the Christian Scriptures
literally.

Christian theologian Michael Goulder pioneered the Midrash interpretation of the Gospels in the
mid-1970's. (5,6) Bishop Spong widely introduced Midrash to the public.
